meta.title: Contoso Web Workload on Azure: Hub-Spoke with Hybrid Admin Access
meta.subtitle: Reference Architecture
meta.description: Customers reach a public web app through an Application Gateway WAF in the hub; the app runs on App Service with private endpoints in a spoke and talks to Azure SQL and Key Vault with managed identities; administrators come in from the Contoso office over VPN through Azure Bastion. Adapted from Microsoft's hub-spoke network topology and App Service baseline reference architectures. The What-If tab shows the same workload with a public Redis cache added in front of SQL, as a proposal to evaluate.
meta.author: DigitalPrez, LLC
meta.revision_note: Two tabs: the baseline, with data classifications on every flow and attack path AP-0001 (exposed jump host to database exfiltration), and a what-if scenario adding a public Redis cache (two threats, three planned controls, AP-0002). Renderer 1.7.0.
meta.objective: Expose one web application to the Internet behind a WAF while keeping data, secrets and administration on private, identity-verified paths.
meta.flow_summary: Customer to web app; administrator to jump VM
meta.access_summary: Customers: Entra ID + MFA (OIDC). Administrators: FIDO2 + Bastion. Services: managed identities. No public endpoints on data or VMs.
assumptions: The Azure landing zone, peering and user-defined routes to the Azure Firewall already exist.
Contoso devices used by administrators are managed and compliant.
Entra ID is operated by the identity team; its internal design is out of scope.
out_of_scope: Disaster recovery to a second region.
The CI/CD pipeline that deploys the application.

steps.name: request
steps.title: A customer reaches the only public entry point
steps.description: The customer's browser resolves the application's public name to the Application Gateway's public IP and opens an HTTPS session. Nothing else in the design has a public address: App Service, SQL, Key Vault and the jump VM are reachable only on private endpoints or through Bastion.
details: TLS terminates at the Application Gateway (WAF v2)
One public IP for the whole workload
PaaS services sit behind private endpoints

steps.name: waf
steps.title: The WAF inspects every request and drops hostile traffic
steps.description: The same endpoint is hit constantly by scanners, credential-stuffing bots and injection attempts. The WAF's OWASP Core Rule Set runs in prevention mode with bot protection, so hostile requests are dropped at the edge and never reach the application.
details: OWASP CRS 3.2 in prevention mode
Bot protection and rate limiting
Blocked requests logged to Log Analytics

steps.name: signin
steps.title: The customer signs in with Entra ID
steps.description: The web front end redirects the customer to Entra ID. Conditional Access requires multifactor authentication; ID Protection evaluates sign-in risk. Entra ID returns an ID token and an access token for the Orders API, which the application validates against the tenant's signing keys.
details: OIDC authorization code flow with PKCE
Conditional Access: MFA for all customers
Risk-based blocking from ID Protection

steps.name: frontend
steps.title: The front end calls the Orders API with the bearer token
steps.description: The Application Gateway forwards the request over end-to-end TLS to the App Service private endpoint. The front end calls the Orders API with the customer's access token; the API validates the token's signature, audience and scopes before doing anything.
details: End-to-end TLS from WAF to private endpoint
Token validation on every API call
FTP and basic-auth deployment disabled on App Service

steps.name: data
steps.title: The API reaches SQL and Key Vault with its managed identity
steps.description: The Orders API uses its system-assigned managed identity: a least-privilege database user in Azure SQL and the Key Vault Secrets User role. There are no connection-string passwords anywhere; both services answer only on private endpoints inside the data subnet, behind an NSG.
details: Managed identity: no stored secrets
Private endpoints; public network access disabled
NSG allows 1433 and 443 from the app subnet only

steps.name: admin
steps.title: An administrator connects from the office over the VPN
steps.description: Administration never comes from the Internet. The administrator signs in to Entra ID with a FIDO2 key, then opens an Azure Bastion session. The traffic leaves the Contoso office through the edge firewall, crosses the IPsec tunnel into the hub VNet's gateway and reaches Bastion on 443.
details: Phishing-resistant MFA for administrators
Bastion session requires Entra sign-in + RBAC on the VM
Site-to-site VPN; no public RDP/SSH anywhere

steps.name: bastion
steps.title: Bastion brokers RDP to the jump VM; direct RDP is denied
steps.description: Bastion opens the RDP session to the jump VM from inside the VNet. The jump VM has no public IP, and its NSG allows 3389 only from the AzureBastionSubnet, so an attacker scanning for exposed RDP finds nothing to connect to.
details: RDP only from the AzureBastionSubnet
Azure Policy denies public IPs on VMs
Just-in-time access and Defender for Servers on the VM

steps.name: dba
steps.title: Database maintenance from the jump VM; the public SQL endpoint stays closed
steps.description: From the jump VM the administrator connects to Azure SQL with Entra ID authentication over the private endpoint. The server's public network access is disabled, so the same connection attempted from the Internet is refused before any authentication happens.
details: Entra-only authentication on SQL
Private endpoint in the data subnet
SQL auditing records every session

steps.name: operate
steps.title: Everything logs to one workspace
steps.description: WAF decisions, firewall and NSG flow logs, App Service diagnostics, SQL auditing and Defender for Cloud alerts all land in the Log Analytics workspace, where Microsoft Sentinel analytics rules watch for credential stuffing, injection and anomalous data access.
details: Diagnostic settings on every resource
Defender for App Service, SQL and Servers
Sentinel analytics on sign-in and data-access anomalies
steps.outcome: Public traffic stops at the WAF, identities are verified by Entra ID, data and secrets stay on private endpoints, and administration is brokered and logged.

threats.title: Credential Stuffing and MFA Fatigue Against Customer Sign-In
threats.description: Bots replay leaked username/password pairs at the Entra sign-in page; where a password matches, repeated push prompts try to wear the customer down into approving one.

attack.scenario: Leaked credential lists are replayed through rotating proxies; successful pairs are escalated to push-bombing.

risk.rationale: Anyone can attempt it and automated tooling is public; MFA keeps most attempts from succeeding but push fatigue works against a share of users.

residual.rationale: Number matching and passkeys (CTL-0002) remove the approve-to-dismiss failure mode; ID Protection blocks risky sign-ins.

provenance.notes: Illustrative example for the reference architecture.

threats.title: SQL Injection Through the Orders API
threats.description: A crafted order query slips past input handling in the API and is executed by Azure SQL with the API's database permissions, exposing or altering other customers' orders.

attack.scenario: An authenticated customer tampers with a search parameter; without parameterization the fragment reaches the database.

risk.rationale: Injection remains among the most attempted web attacks; the data is restricted.

residual.rationale: WAF rules (CTL-0003) plus parameterized queries and a least-privilege database user (CTL-0004), verified by penetration test.

provenance.notes: Illustrative example for the reference architecture.

threats.title: SSRF from the API Reaches the Instance Metadata Service and Steals a Managed-Identity Token
threats.description: If the API can be made to fetch an attacker-chosen URL, it can be pointed at the Azure Instance Metadata Service and asked for an access token for its own managed identity; that token then works against Key Vault and SQL from anywhere.

attack.scenario: A webhook or import feature in the API accepts a URL; the attacker supplies the IMDS token endpoint and reads the response.
prerequisites: A server-side fetch of user-supplied URLs

risk.rationale: SSRF is a design flaw that appears regularly; a stolen managed-identity token bypasses the network controls entirely.

residual.rationale: Least-privilege RBAC (CTL-0006) limits what a stolen token can do; Defender alerts (CTL-0007) catch anomalous Key Vault access. An outbound URL allow-list in the API is still open.

provenance.notes: Illustrative example for the reference architecture.

threats.title: NSG Drift Exposes RDP on the Jump VM to the Internet
threats.description: A troubleshooting rule that allows 3389 from Any, or a public IP attached during an incident, would put a domain-joined administration host directly on the Internet.
assets_at_risk: Azure SQL via the DBA path

attack.scenario: Internet-wide RDP scanners find the port within minutes; password spraying follows.
prerequisites: An NSG rule or public IP added outside the pipeline

risk.rationale: Drift happens, but policy and monitoring make it short-lived; the host is a direct path to data.

residual.rationale: Azure Policy denies public IPs (CTL-0009) and the Bastion-only NSG baseline is continuously monitored (CTL-0008).

provenance.notes: Illustrative example for the reference architecture.

threats.title: Saved Database Connections on the Jump VM Turn a Foothold into Data Access
threats.description: Administrators keep SQL Server Management Studio connections with cached Entra tokens on the jump VM. Anyone who lands an interactive session on the VM can open the Orders database as the last administrator without a fresh prompt.

vulnerability.description: Saved connections and cached tokens on a shared administration host.

attack.scenario: With a session on the jump VM the attacker opens SSMS, picks the saved production connection and queries the Orders tables; the private endpoint and the NSG see an ordinary administrator session.
prerequisites: An interactive session on the jump VM (see THR-0004)

risk.rationale: Saved connections are the norm on administration hosts; the data behind them is the asset everything else protects.

residual.rationale: Bastion-only access and just-in-time make the prerequisite session rare, but nothing on the VM itself stops the reuse.

projected.rationale: With no saved connections and MFA on every SQL sign-in the foothold yields nothing.

controls.name: Conditional Access Requires MFA for All Customer Sign-Ins
Number Matching and Passkeys for Customers
WAF V2 with OWASP CRS 3.2 in Prevention Mode and Bot Protection
Parameterized Queries and a Least-Privilege SQL Role for the API Identity
Entra ID Protection Sign-In Risk Policies
Least-Privilege Key Vault RBAC; No Secrets in App Settings
Defender for App Service and Defender for SQL Alerts into Sentinel
Bastion-Only Administration; NSG Denies Inbound 3389/22 from Anywhere Else
Azure Policy Denies Public IPs on VMs and Public Network Access on PaaS
No Saved Database Connections on the Jump VM; MFA on Every SQL Sign-In
controls.description: Remove saved SSMS connections and cached tokens by policy (connection history disabled, no roaming profiles), require a fresh Entra MFA prompt for every SQL administrator sign-in, and alert on SQL sessions from the jump VM outside a change window.

attack_paths.title: Exposed Jump Host to Database Exfiltration
attack_paths.description: A drifted NSG rule exposes RDP on the jump VM; a password spray lands a session; the saved SSMS connection opens the Orders database; the data leaves through the RDP session.

hops.note: Internet-wide scanners find the exposed 3389 within minutes; a password spray against the local administrator account lands an interactive session.
The saved SSMS connection authenticates as the last DBA; the private endpoint and the NSG see an ordinary administration session.
Query results are copied out through the RDP session (clipboard, mapped drive); nothing on the path inspects outbound RDP content.

attack_paths.impact: Customer orders and PII copied out of Azure SQL through an administration host: regulatory notification and card-brand exposure.

risk.rationale: The chain needs the NSG to drift and the spray to succeed before the saved connection matters.

residual.rationale: Bastion-only administration and the deny rule make hop 1 unlikely; hop 2 is open.

projected.rationale: With no saved connections the foothold yields no data; what is left is the VM itself.

steps.title: A customer reaches the only public entry point
steps.description: The customer's browser resolves the application's public name to the Application Gateway's public IP and opens an HTTPS session. Nothing else in the design has a public address: App Service, SQL, Key Vault and the jump VM are reachable only on private endpoints or through Bastion.
details: TLS terminates at the Application Gateway (WAF v2)
One public IP for the whole workload
PaaS services sit behind private endpoints

steps.name: waf
steps.title: The WAF inspects every request and drops hostile traffic
steps.description: The same endpoint is hit constantly by scanners, credential-stuffing bots and injection attempts. The WAF's OWASP Core Rule Set runs in prevention mode with bot protection, so hostile requests are dropped at the edge and never reach the application.
details: OWASP CRS 3.2 in prevention mode
Bot protection and rate limiting
Blocked requests logged to Log Analytics

steps.name: signin
steps.title: The customer signs in with Entra ID
steps.description: The web front end redirects the customer to Entra ID. Conditional Access requires multifactor authentication; ID Protection evaluates sign-in risk. Entra ID returns an ID token and an access token for the Orders API, which the application validates against the tenant's signing keys.
details: OIDC authorization code flow with PKCE
Conditional Access: MFA for all customers
Risk-based blocking from ID Protection

steps.name: frontend
steps.title: The front end calls the Orders API with the bearer token
steps.description: The Application Gateway forwards the request over end-to-end TLS to the App Service private endpoint. The front end calls the Orders API with the customer's access token; the API validates the token's signature, audience and scopes before doing anything.
details: End-to-end TLS from WAF to private endpoint
Token validation on every API call
FTP and basic-auth deployment disabled on App Service

steps.name: data
steps.title: The API reaches SQL and Key Vault with its managed identity
steps.description: The Orders API uses its system-assigned managed identity: a least-privilege database user in Azure SQL and the Key Vault Secrets User role. There are no connection-string passwords anywhere; both services answer only on private endpoints inside the data subnet, behind an NSG.
details: Managed identity: no stored secrets
Private endpoints; public network access disabled
NSG allows 1433 and 443 from the app subnet only

steps.name: cache
steps.title: The API reads from the public cache first; the Internet can reach the same endpoint
steps.description: With the change applied, order reads go to Azure Cache for Redis and fall back to SQL on a miss. The cache was deployed with its public endpoint enabled and access-key authentication, so the same endpoint the API uses is reachable from the Internet by anyone who holds the key.
details: Access key in App Service configuration and the pipeline
Public endpoint: the NSG does not apply
Cached records bypass SQL auditing and row-level security

steps.name: admin
steps.title: An administrator connects from the office over the VPN
steps.description: Administration never comes from the Internet. The administrator signs in to Entra ID with a FIDO2 key, then opens an Azure Bastion session. The traffic leaves the Contoso office through the edge firewall, crosses the IPsec tunnel into the hub VNet's gateway and reaches Bastion on 443.
details: Phishing-resistant MFA for administrators
Bastion session requires Entra sign-in + RBAC on the VM
Site-to-site VPN; no public RDP/SSH anywhere

steps.name: bastion
steps.title: Bastion brokers RDP to the jump VM; direct RDP is denied
steps.description: Bastion opens the RDP session to the jump VM from inside the VNet. The jump VM has no public IP, and its NSG allows 3389 only from the AzureBastionSubnet, so an attacker scanning for exposed RDP finds nothing to connect to.
details: RDP only from the AzureBastionSubnet
Azure Policy denies public IPs on VMs
Just-in-time access and Defender for Servers on the VM

steps.name: dba
steps.title: Database maintenance from the jump VM; the public SQL endpoint stays closed
steps.description: From the jump VM the administrator connects to Azure SQL with Entra ID authentication over the private endpoint. The server's public network access is disabled, so the same connection attempted from the Internet is refused before any authentication happens.
details: Entra-only authentication on SQL
Private endpoint in the data subnet
SQL auditing records every session

steps.name: operate
steps.title: Everything logs to one workspace
steps.description: WAF decisions, firewall and NSG flow logs, App Service diagnostics, SQL auditing and Defender for Cloud alerts all land in the Log Analytics workspace, where Microsoft Sentinel analytics rules watch for credential stuffing, injection and anomalous data access.
details: Diagnostic settings on every resource
Defender for App Service, SQL and Servers
Sentinel analytics on sign-in and data-access anomalies
steps.outcome: Public traffic stops at the WAF, identities are verified by Entra ID, data and secrets stay on private endpoints, and administration is brokered and logged.

threats.title: Credential Stuffing and MFA Fatigue Against Customer Sign-In
threats.description: Bots replay leaked username/password pairs at the Entra sign-in page; where a password matches, repeated push prompts try to wear the customer down into approving one.

attack.scenario: Leaked credential lists are replayed through rotating proxies; successful pairs are escalated to push-bombing.

risk.rationale: Anyone can attempt it and automated tooling is public; MFA keeps most attempts from succeeding but push fatigue works against a share of users.

residual.rationale: Number matching and passkeys (CTL-0002) remove the approve-to-dismiss failure mode; ID Protection blocks risky sign-ins.

provenance.notes: Illustrative example for the reference architecture.

threats.title: SQL Injection Through the Orders API
threats.description: A crafted order query slips past input handling in the API and is executed by Azure SQL with the API's database permissions, exposing or altering other customers' orders.

attack.scenario: An authenticated customer tampers with a search parameter; without parameterization the fragment reaches the database.

risk.rationale: Injection remains among the most attempted web attacks; the data is restricted.

residual.rationale: WAF rules (CTL-0003) plus parameterized queries and a least-privilege database user (CTL-0004), verified by penetration test.

provenance.notes: Illustrative example for the reference architecture.

threats.title: SSRF from the API Reaches the Instance Metadata Service and Steals a Managed-Identity Token
threats.description: If the API can be made to fetch an attacker-chosen URL, it can be pointed at the Azure Instance Metadata Service and asked for an access token for its own managed identity; that token then works against Key Vault and SQL from anywhere.

attack.scenario: A webhook or import feature in the API accepts a URL; the attacker supplies the IMDS token endpoint and reads the response.
prerequisites: A server-side fetch of user-supplied URLs

risk.rationale: SSRF is a design flaw that appears regularly; a stolen managed-identity token bypasses the network controls entirely.

residual.rationale: Least-privilege RBAC (CTL-0006) limits what a stolen token can do; Defender alerts (CTL-0007) catch anomalous Key Vault access. An outbound URL allow-list in the API is still open.

provenance.notes: Illustrative example for the reference architecture.

threats.title: NSG Drift Exposes RDP on the Jump VM to the Internet
threats.description: A troubleshooting rule that allows 3389 from Any, or a public IP attached during an incident, would put a domain-joined administration host directly on the Internet.
assets_at_risk: Azure SQL via the DBA path

attack.scenario: Internet-wide RDP scanners find the port within minutes; password spraying follows.
prerequisites: An NSG rule or public IP added outside the pipeline

risk.rationale: Drift happens, but policy and monitoring make it short-lived; the host is a direct path to data.

residual.rationale: Azure Policy denies public IPs (CTL-0009) and the Bastion-only NSG baseline is continuously monitored (CTL-0008).

provenance.notes: Illustrative example for the reference architecture.

threats.title: Saved Database Connections on the Jump VM Turn a Foothold into Data Access
threats.description: Administrators keep SQL Server Management Studio connections with cached Entra tokens on the jump VM. Anyone who lands an interactive session on the VM can open the Orders database as the last administrator without a fresh prompt.

vulnerability.description: Saved connections and cached tokens on a shared administration host.

attack.scenario: With a session on the jump VM the attacker opens SSMS, picks the saved production connection and queries the Orders tables; the private endpoint and the NSG see an ordinary administrator session.
prerequisites: An interactive session on the jump VM (see THR-0004)

risk.rationale: Saved connections are the norm on administration hosts; the data behind them is the asset everything else protects.

residual.rationale: Bastion-only access and just-in-time make the prerequisite session rare, but nothing on the VM itself stops the reuse.

projected.rationale: With no saved connections and MFA on every SQL sign-in the foothold yields nothing.

threats.title: Public Redis Endpoint Reachable from the Internet with a Shared Access Key
threats.description: The cache answers on a public endpoint and the access key is the only credential. The key lives in App Service configuration and pipeline variables; a leak, a repository export or a departing engineer gives a direct, unaudited read of every cached record from anywhere.

vulnerability.description: Public network access enabled; shared-key authentication without identity.

attack.scenario: The key is found in a leaked pipeline log or a misconfigured repository; redis-cli connects to the public endpoint over TLS and walks the keyspace.

risk.rationale: Shared keys leak; the endpoint is one DNS lookup away.

projected.rationale: Private endpoint only and Entra authentication remove both the reachability and the shared secret.

threats.title: Cached Order Records Bypass SQL Row-Level Security and Auditing
threats.description: Records that SQL protects with row-level security, auditing and Entra-only authentication sit in the cache as plain keys for up to 15 minutes; anyone with the key reads across customers and nothing records the read.

vulnerability.description: A second copy of restricted data with weaker controls than the system of record.

risk.rationale: Follows directly from any read of the cache; the design copies the most sensitive records into a weaker store.

projected.rationale: Caching only non-sensitive projections with a short TTL leaves little to read.

controls.name: Conditional Access Requires MFA for All Customer Sign-Ins
Number Matching and Passkeys for Customers
WAF V2 with OWASP CRS 3.2 in Prevention Mode and Bot Protection
Parameterized Queries and a Least-Privilege SQL Role for the API Identity
Entra ID Protection Sign-In Risk Policies
Least-Privilege Key Vault RBAC; No Secrets in App Settings
Defender for App Service and Defender for SQL Alerts into Sentinel
Bastion-Only Administration; NSG Denies Inbound 3389/22 from Anywhere Else
Azure Policy Denies Public IPs on VMs and Public Network Access on PaaS
No Saved Database Connections on the Jump VM; MFA on Every SQL Sign-In
controls.description: Remove saved SSMS connections and cached tokens by policy (connection history disabled, no roaming profiles), require a fresh Entra MFA prompt for every SQL administrator sign-in, and alert on SQL sessions from the jump VM outside a change window.

controls.name: Private Endpoint Only: Public Network Access Disabled on the Cache
controls.description: Deploy the cache with a private endpoint in the data subnet and public network access disabled; Azure Policy (CTL-0009) denies the public setting.

controls.name: Entra ID Authentication for Redis; Access Keys Disabled
controls.description: Turn on Microsoft Entra authentication for the cache, grant the API's managed identity the data-reader role, disable access-key authentication and rotate the existing keys out of configuration and the pipeline.

controls.name: Cache Only Non-Sensitive Projections; 60-Second TTL for Anything with PII
controls.description: Cache catalogue and status projections, not customer records; where a PII field must be cached, key it per customer, hash the lookup and expire it in 60 seconds; log cache reads of PII keys to Log Analytics.

attack_paths.title: Exposed Jump Host to Database Exfiltration
attack_paths.description: A drifted NSG rule exposes RDP on the jump VM; a password spray lands a session; the saved SSMS connection opens the Orders database; the data leaves through the RDP session.

hops.note: Internet-wide scanners find the exposed 3389 within minutes; a password spray against the local administrator account lands an interactive session.
The saved SSMS connection authenticates as the last DBA; the private endpoint and the NSG see an ordinary administration session.
Query results are copied out through the RDP session (clipboard, mapped drive); nothing on the path inspects outbound RDP content.

attack_paths.impact: Customer orders and PII copied out of Azure SQL through an administration host: regulatory notification and card-brand exposure.

risk.rationale: The chain needs the NSG to drift and the spray to succeed before the saved connection matters.

residual.rationale: Bastion-only administration and the deny rule make hop 1 unlikely; hop 2 is open.

projected.rationale: With no saved connections the foothold yields no data; what is left is the VM itself.

attack_paths.title: Leaked Cache Key to Customer Data
attack_paths.description: The shared access key leaks from configuration or a pipeline log; the public endpoint answers from anywhere; the keyspace is walked and up to 15 minutes of order and customer records are read outside SQL auditing.

hops.note: With the leaked key, redis-cli connects to the public endpoint over TLS; there is no identity, no conditional access and no NSG in the way.
SCAN and DUMP walk every cached order and customer record across tenants; the cache has no row-level security and records no reads.

attack_paths.impact: Up to 15 minutes of order and customer records readable by anyone holding the key, from anywhere, with no audit trail.

risk.rationale: Two steps, both easy once the key is out; keys of this kind leak regularly.

projected.rationale: A private endpoint with Entra authentication removes hop 1; projections with a short TTL leave little behind for hop 2.

scenario.change: Replace the direct Azure SQL read path with an Azure Cache for Redis for read-through caching, deployed with its public endpoint enabled and access-key authentication.
scenario.author: DigitalPrez, LLC
assumptions: The cache holds customer and order records for up to 15 minutes.
The access key is stored in App Service configuration and in the deployment pipeline.

tabs.flow_summary: Customer to web app; API to cache, SQL on a miss; administrator to jump VM
